subject: humanities
passage: Braille, the raised-dot system that lets blind people read by touch, was developed in France by Louis Braille, who lost his sight as a young child. As a student, he learned of a code of raised dots invented by an army officer, Charles Barbier, so that messages could be read in the dark. Braille found the code too complicated, so he simplified it. By age fifteen, he had created a system in which each letter fit under a single fingertip.
stem: According to the text, what did Louis Braille do with Barbier's code?

choices.A: He taught it to soldiers who needed to read at night.
choices.B: He simplified it to create an easier system.
choices.C: He replaced its raised dots with printed letters.
choices.D: He decided it was simple enough to use without changes.

explanation.why: The text says Braille "found the code too complicated, so he simplified it," creating a system in which each letter fit under one fingertip. The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Barbier invented the code for reading in the dark, but the text never says Braille taught soldiers.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates "he simplified it," which led to his own easier system.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Braille's own system still uses raised dots, as the first sentence says; nothing was replaced with printed letters.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Braille found the code "too complicated," so he did change it.
